definition: HYPO is a computer program, an expert system, that models reasoning with cases and hypotheticals in the legal domain.
details: It is the first of its kind and the most sophisticated of the case-based legal reasoners, which was designed by Kevin Ashley for his Ph.D dissertation in 1987 at the University of Massachusetts Amherst under the supervision of Edwina Rissland. HYPO's design represents a hybrid generalization/comparative evaluation method appropriate for a domain with a weak analytical theory and applies to tasks that rarely involve just one right answer. The domain covers US trade secret law, and is substantially a common law domain. Since Anglo-American common law operates under the doctrine of precedent, the definitive way of interpreting problems is of necessity and case-based. Thus, HYPO did not involve the analysis of a statute, as required by the Prolog program. Rissland and Ashley (1987) envisioned HYPO as employing the key tasks performed by lawyers when analyzing case law for precedence to generate arguments for the prosecution or the defence. story: Imagine a mathematician who writes every step on paper, reads it back, crosses out a bad line, and starts that line over. Slowing down to think often beats answering fast. Instead of blurting out an answer, the machine talks its way through the problem one step at a time. More time spent reconsidering can be worth more than a bigger model. And that habit of thinking twice — or a hundred times — is HYPO CBR.
